title: How to psychologicaly recover from an injury
summary: NH covers the mental side of injury: guilt or betrayal create negative energy, fear makes you stiff and can create pain, and the brain must relearn that a movement is safe. Using his broken-ribs squat injury as an example, he advises a slow, methodical return, retaking weights, treating the injury weight as the key milestone, and never getting injured twice the same way.

claims.claim: The psychological side of recovering from injury is under-discussed and sometimes more important than what you do physically.
After an injury people feel either betrayed by their body or guilty for neglecting recovery, nutrition, volume and intensity management; both are negative energy.
Healing takes mental strength: if you don't believe you'll heal you won't; a strong will to recover matters, as seen with seriously ill people.

Complaining about an injury means you aren't working on it; for most injuries (except e.g. a snapped tendon needing surgery) you should keep moving to get blood flowing and strengthen surrounding muscles.
Injury takes your confidence and makes you afraid, and fear is the enemy of progress.
Fear tends to plague the specific movement you got hurt on: you get stiff, expect pain, and can create the pain yourself.

NH broke (snapped) ribs squatting; after rehab pain persisted, and his doctor said ribs and muscles had healed and he had taught himself that the movement causes pain. He had to unlearn it by doing the movement and telling himself he wasn't broken.
The most important milestone when rebuilding an injured lift is the weight you got injured on; conquering it yields huge gains in mental strength, while a weight just below it will feel easy.
Return to pre-injury strength slowly and methodically; rushing because you feel you lost time is the best way to get re-injured.
Getting injured once is okay; getting injured twice doing the same thing is stupid, because it creates a chronic injury pattern that is much harder to break.
A common mistake: after a deadlift injury people tighten form, then let it slip again to get stronger and get re-injured; respect your body, because repeated injuries can damage it for life.
Don't hesitate to retake weights if technique or strength isn't there; there is no rush.
For a bodybuilder, strength is just a number multiplied by reps to get tonnage; steady slow progress beats a cycle of progress-injury-setback.
The best set with the weight that injured you is one that feels non-challenging; once done, the fear is exorcised and becomes easy to repeat.
Rehab successes create a virtuous circle; small victories count, like retaking a deadlift weight without lower-back or SI-joint pain, accumulating tonnage instead of damage.
For NH, strength of mind is as important as strength of body.
